patna-ganga-riverfront-resettlement.confidence_note: The two deaths at Beur in May 2021 are now recorded outside the lender. The Caravan of 15 September 2021 names the dead as Saddam Hussien, 20, and Mohammed Iqbal Hussain, 18, both from Bhagwangola in Murshidabad district, West Bengal, puts them in a sewer at the Namami Gange works in the Beur locality of Patna on 31 May 2021, and gives the chain of employment as BUIDCo to Larsen and Toubro to a Murshidabad subcontractor, Nayan Raza; Maktoob Media of 1 July 2021 reports a fact-finding visit by the Dalit Adivasi Shakti Adhikar Manch and Loktantrik Jan Pahal, which held the company and contractor responsible and said an FIR should have been registered against them, and records that the police instead registered an unnatural-death FIR, number 15/21. The Comptroller and Auditor General's audit of the Namami Gange works in Bihar, for the year ended March 2020, independently names BUIDCo as executing agency and Larsen and Toubro as the firm laying the Beur sewerage network, and records cracks and leaks at the Beur plant on physical verification in January 2021. The Bank's own completion report lists Patna Beur sewerage works and Begusarai sewerage and STP among the project's investments, which is what ties these works to the credit: no outside document read names the World Bank, and the Caravan attributes the Beur sanction to a Rs 398 crore allocation by the Ministry of Jal Shakti of 6 April 2017. Two outlets give different names for the dead: the Caravan gives Saddam Hussien and Mohammed Iqbal Hussain, Maktoob Media gives Mohamad Idrish and Mohamad Iqbal. On procurement, the Patna High Court in M/s EMS Infracon Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Bihar, CWJC No. 9597 of 2021, decided 19 July 2021, set aside BUIDCo's blacklisting of a bidder for the Munger sewage treatment plant and 167.3 km sewerage network under this credit, found that BUIDCo had "acted irresponsibly in passing the impugned order in casual and cavalier manner", recorded that three blacklisting orders against bidders on the same invitation for bids by the same Chief Engineer had been quashed, and ordered a fresh technical bid evaluation chaired by the Development Commissioner with the Mission's Executive Director (Technical) on the committee. The riverfront resettlement itself is unchanged: the 249 families, the two-year stall in the land allotment, the handing of sites to the contractor before people were resettled and paid, and the Begusarai death in March 2021 still rest on the Bank's completion report alone. Indian Kanoon holds no judgment on the Patna riverfront development or on the deaths; the only Ganga-pollution matter that names this programme, M C Mehta v. Union of India before the National Green Tribunal, records neither.

field_changes.killed_note: Three deaths, from the Bank's completion report: one at Begusarai in March 2021 and two at Beur in May 2021, at sites the same report lists among the project's investments. The two Beur deaths are recorded outside the lender. The Caravan of 15 September 2021 puts them in a sewer at the Namami Gange works in Beur, Patna, on 31 May 2021, names them as Saddam Hussien, 20, and Mohammed Iqbal Hussain, 18, both from Bhagwangola in Murshidabad district, West Bengal, and traces the work from BUIDCo to Larsen and Toubro to a subcontractor, Nayan Raza. Maktoob Media of 1 July 2021 gives the names as Mohamad Idrish and Mohamad Iqbal and records that the police registered an unnatural-death FIR, 15/21, rather than a culpable homicide case. The Begusarai death of March 2021 appears in no document outside the Bank's report that was read.

corrections: The completion report says of the three deaths that "the next-of-kin were duly compensated" and, in its risk section, that compensation to the next of kin "were fully paid". For the two Beur deaths that was not true for at least three and a half months: the fact-finding report carried by Maktoob Media on 1 July 2021 says no compensation had been paid, and the Caravan, reporting from Patna on 15 September 2021, says the families had received nothing and that "by mid September, no culpable homicide case had been registered". The completion report of 28 February 2023 may be describing payments made later; it gives no date, and it does not mention that the police registered only an unnatural-death FIR.

The card's place field and its account of the deaths treat Beur as part of the riverfront works. They are separate investments: the completion report's investment table lists 'Patna: River Front Development' and 'Patna Beur: Sewerage works' as different contracts, and the two men died in a sewer on the Beur sewerage network, not at the riverfront.
patna-ganga-riverfront-resettlement.what_the_outside_source_settles: That two labourers died in a sewer on the Namami Gange works in Beur, Patna, on 31 May 2021; who they were, where they came from and how old they were; who held the contract and who sublet it; that the police treated the deaths as unnatural deaths rather than as a crime by the company; and that no compensation had reached the families by mid-September 2021. Separately, that the Munger bid evaluation under this credit was defective enough for the Patna High Court to quash the blacklisting of a bidder and order the evaluation done again, and that three blacklisting orders by the same Chief Engineer on the same invitation for bids were found illegal.
patna-ganga-riverfront-resettlement.what_it_does_not_settle: Nothing about the riverfront resettlement: no outside document read names the 249 families, the stalled land allotment, the extra cash paid instead of land, or the handing of sites to the contractor before people were resettled. Nothing about the death at Begusarai in March 2021. And no outside document names the World Bank as financier of the Beur works: the Caravan traces the money to a Rs 398 crore sanction by the Ministry of Jal Shakti in April 2017 and the Comptroller and Auditor General treats the Bihar works as centrally funded Namami Gange, so the link between these deaths and this credit still comes from the Bank's own investment table. The court judgment does not mention the leak of confidential information that the completion report reports for the Munger evaluation; it found different defects in the same procurement.

karnataka-state-highways-ii-compensation.confidence_note: Two outside documents now carry part of this harm. The High Court of Karnataka at Dharwad, on 24 November 2021, decided MFA No. 102520/2017 and 28 connected appeals brought by the Assistant Commissioner (Land Acquisition), Karnataka State Highway Improvement Project, against landowners of Karagudari village, Hangal taluk, Haveri district, whose land was taken under a final notification of 10 January 2011 for the link road between State Highway 1 and State Highway 69 from Hangal to Tadas, Link No. M7D. The Bank's completion report lists M7D Hangal-Tadasa, 43.5 km, as package WEP-2B of this project, with works running from 6 July 2013 to 31 January 2017, which is what identifies the road. The general award was passed on 30 April 2011; the owners went to the reference court at Hangal, which in a common judgment of 2 November 2016 fixed the market value at Rs 44,000 per gunta; the state appealed, and the High Court cut it, holding that "market value of the said lands is fixed at Rs.35,000/- per gunta", following a coordinate bench judgment of 20 February 2021 on Nitaginakoppa lands under the same notification. Ten and a half years passed between the award and the final figure, and the state's appeal lowered what the reference court had allowed. Second, the Comptroller and Auditor General of India, auditing Karnataka's public sector undertakings for the year ended 31 March 2019, examined the six roads the Karnataka Road Development Corporation built under this loan and found "delay in initiation of land acquisition in respect of six projects": the roads were identified in May 2011 and the loan and project agreements with the IBRD concluded in that month, but the corporation began acquisition only between September 2014 and October 2017, final notifications for possession ran from August 2016 to February 2019, and the Resettlement Action Plan was approved only in 2015. Audit attributed this to the late formation of the land acquisition cell in 2012 and the late engagement of staff in 2014. A third document, Kumaraswamy J R and others v. The Project Director, Project Implementation Unit, KSHIP, WP No. 16880 of 2022, decided 2 January 2023, records three brothers of Jinnagara village, Kunigal taluk, Tumkur district whose land had been acquired and whose repeated representations about compensation had gone unanswered; the court gave the project three months to decide them, warning that lapsing officials would be personally liable for costs. The order does not name the road, so the parcel is not tied to this project beyond the acquiring authority, though the completion report lists links 63C Huliyurdurga-Kunigal and 63D Kunigal-Tumkur among its roads. The rest of the card is unchanged and still rests on the Bank's documents and on the two impact evaluations the project commissioned: the 602 acres and 6,800 landowners, the 2,200 informal occupiers, the 200 households displaced, the income tax deducted from 7 and 67 people's compensation, the 40 per cent of compensation deposited in the courts, and the two named villages. The Comptroller and Auditor General's paragraphs about Rs 180 crore of unpaid compensation and awards delayed 13 to 23 months are about the Yelahanka to Andhra Pradesh border road, which the same chapter treats as a project of the corporation outside the World Bank co-financing, and are not used here.

andhra-pradesh-community-forest.confidence_note: Indian Kanoon holds no judgment on the evictions. An independent Indian review does carry part of the harm: Working Paper No. 62 of the Centre for Economic and Social Studies, Hyderabad, of October 2004, by V. Ratna Reddy, M. Gopinath Reddy, Velayutham Saravanan, Madhusudana Bandhii and Oliver Springate-Baginski, reviews participatory forest management in Andhra Pradesh and treats the Bank's project as its main funder, giving it 2,910 of the state's forest protection committees against 1,956 under the Employment Assurance Scheme and 918 under NABARD, and dating the first phase to 1994 to September 2000. On the harm it records, citing Rangachari and Mukherji (2000), the return to the Forest Department of about 24,000 hectares of land that had been under podu cultivation, most of it in the committees of Visakhapatnam and Adilabad districts, and comments that while the department treats this as a success, "land has been taken out of use for livelihood support of tribals". It records that in the mainly tribal Paderu division tribal organisations rejected the second-phase community forest management approach for fear of losing more podu land, and that in Paderu villagers felt the department was setting one village against another by granting one village rights over a neighbour's forest on condition that podu cultivation stopped. It distinguishes those who gave up podu land and still had private land to live on from those "facing forced eviction in plain terrain where podu cultivation has almost become permanent cultivation". On numbers it gives, citing Madhusudhan (2003), an estimated 46,725 families who may have been cultivating forestland assigned to the committees, of whom the second-phase Resettlement Action Plan provided a rehabilitation grant and livelihood opportunities to an estimated 11,680, which is close to the 28 per cent of people in project areas the Bank expected to affect. These are figures the review takes from other authors, not its own field counts, and the review is an academic survey rather than a judgment or an audit, so it does not settle the dispute on the card between Samata's account of coercion and the forest department's account of voluntary departure; it reports both readings itself. On the judgment route, the only matter Indian Kanoon returns for the project is Divisional Forest Officer, Kothagudem v. Madhusudhan Rao, decided by the Supreme Court on 8 February 2008, which names the Andhra Pradesh Forestry Project only as the source of the funds a forester was charged with embezzling, including Rs 4,865 of unpaid labourers' wages; it records nothing about this card's harm to these people in these forests. The nearest judgment on the facts, Sreeramanjaneyapuram Village Society v. Divisional Forest Officer, Guntur, decided by the Andhra Pradesh High Court on 18 April 2003, dismissed a claim to one hectare each for 400 Banjara, Sugali and Dalit families whose possession of forest land at Venkatayapalem had been formalised through a forest protection committee account that was later cancelled, and recorded the government's case that the members "who encroached upon the forest land, have already been evicted". It is the same scheme and the same state inside the project years, but the judgment names neither the project nor the Bank, and Bellamkonda in Guntur is not one of the tribal forest areas on this card, so it cannot be treated as the same people or the same parcel.

andhra-pradesh-community-forest.what_the_outside_source_settles: That land under podu cultivation was taken out of tribal use on a large scale under the forest protection committee programme this project financed, on the order of 24,000 hectares in committee areas concentrated in Visakhapatnam and Adilabad; that the second-phase Resettlement Action Plan covered a minority of the families estimated to be cultivating the forestland assigned to committees; and that tribal organisations in Paderu refused the second phase for fear of losing more podu land. andhra-pradesh-community-forest.what_it_does_not_settle: Whether the departures were coerced. The review reports both the department's account and the critics' and uses the words voluntary and forced of different groups, so the central dispute on the card stands. It names no family, gives no date for any eviction, and gives no compensation figure. No judgment, state audit or gazette notice recording an eviction under this project was found.

LesothoLII was searched through its API for the works, the places and the parties: 'Nyenye', 'Makhoroana', 'Nyenye-Makhoroana', 'Makhoroana road', 'Mapoteng', 'Teyateyaneng to Mapoteng', 'Senqunyane', 'Integrated Transport Project', 'Ministry of Public Works and Transport', 'Roads Directorate', 'expropriation of land', 'compensation for land', 'compensation for crops', 'resettlement' and 'road construction compensation'. It holds no judgment about these works. The two phrases naming the project's own roads return nothing; 'compensation for crops' returns only section 54 of the Land Act 2010; 'resettlement' returns five documents, the nearest of them a Labour Court case against the Lesotho Highlands Development Authority. The ministry cases that the phrase search does return are about other things: Tsalong v. Principal Secretary, Ministry of Public Works and Transport, CIV/APN/398/13, decided 30 October 2017, is a dismissal from the Department of Traffic and Transport after a forensic audit, with no land in it; Nchere v. Roads Directorate, CIV/T/504/19, decided 11 November 2019, is a default judgment of M149,053 for a pedestrian who fell into an unprotected pit beside the main North 1 road near the Mookoli T junction, with no project named and no land, crops or households. The candidate the batch supplied, Ministry of Public Works and Transport and others v. Lesotho Consolidated Civil Contractors (Pty) Ltd, C of A (CIV) 9 of 2014, decided 17 April 2014, is the trap it looks like: it is about the termination on 21 November 2012 of a contract of 18 November 2008 worth M212,771,071.27 for upgrading the road from Likalaneng to Thaba-Tseka, a road that is not on this card, and it mentions no lender, no land, no crops, no households and no resettlement. The harm on this card remains two households resettled, an unnumbered set of farmland strips compensated for bus and taxi bays, culverts that damaged farmland, and a small number of market stalls moved at Makhoroana, all of it the lender's own account, with no resettlement completion report in existence.
